# ![[Uncaptioned image]]()MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Framework For Text-To-SQL

Haolin Yang Affiliation: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
   Jipeng Zhang Affiliation: Hong Kong University of Science and
Technology    Zhitao He Affiliation: Hong Kong University of Science and
Technology    Alexander Zhou Affiliation: Hong Kong Polytechnic
University    Yi R. (May) Fung Affiliation: Hong Kong University of
Science and Technology Correspondence to: <yrfung@ust.hk>

###### Abstract

Large Language Models (LLMs) often struggle with the precise logic and
schema alignment required for complex Text-to-SQL tasks. While current
methods rely heavily on static prompting, they lack the ability to
dynamically adapt and self-correct through environmental interaction. To
bridge this gap, we propose MARS-SQL, a trainable multi-agent framework
for Text-to-SQL. Rather than introducing a new standalone SQL primitive,
MARS-SQL makes an agentic workflow trainable by decomposing the problem
into three specialized roles: schema grounding, query generation, and
solution validation. Central to our approach is a generation agent
trained via a multi-turn RL policy within a ReAct-style loop. The agent
learns to iteratively reason, execute intermediate SQL actions on a live
database, and refine its strategy based on execution feedback. To
improve robustness, we further introduce a validation mechanism that
treats solution selection as a generative modeling task, identifying the
optimal interaction trajectory through next-token prediction
probabilities. Empirical evaluations demonstrate the effectiveness of
coupling interactive learning with trajectory ranking. MARS-SQL achieves
state-of-the-art performance, recording an execution accuracy of 77.84%
on the BIRD development dataset and 89.75% on the Spider test dataset,
while also transferring strongly to out-of-domain benchmarks. Code is
available at
[https://github.com/YangHaolin0526/MARS-SQL](https://github.com/YangHaolin0526/MARS-SQL).

## 1 Introduction

Translating natural language questions into executable Structured Query
Language (SQL) is an essential task that allows non-expert users to
access structured data ([Xie et al., 2025b](#bib.bib1); [Li et al.,
2024a](#bib.bib62); [Li et al., 2023](#bib.bib24)). Recent Large
Language Models (LLMs) can generate simple queries for well-organised
academic benchmarks. However, they often struggle with the complexity of
real-world enterprise databases ([Hong et al., 2025](#bib.bib27); [Lei
et al., 2025](#bib.bib49)). To bridge this gap and tackle the challenges
of interacting with complex, real-world databases, researchers have
started developing SQL agents ([Li et al., 2025b](#bib.bib67); [Wang et
al., 2025b](#bib.bib68); [Li et al., 2025c](#bib.bib70)). Instead of
producing a query in one step, an SQL agent allows an LLM to interact
with the database through multiple rounds of reasoning and feedback.
This interactive process resembles how human analysts explore data,
making it a more natural and effective way to handle complex database
tasks.

Current methodologies in the broader field of AI agents have explored
several distinct avenues. A prominent strategy is the use of multi-agent
systems, where a complex task is decomposed into specialized sub-tasks,
each handled by a dedicated agent ([Chang et al., 2025](#bib.bib39);
[Huang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib69); [Liu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib12);
[Huang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib11)). A parallel line of work uses
test-time scaling methods that generate multiple candidate queries and
then select the best one ([Ni et al., 2023](#bib.bib64); [Li et al.,
2022](#bib.bib65)). In the specific domain of Text-to-SQL, these
methodologies manifest in two primary forms. One approach relies on
monolithic models, which handle schema comprehension, logical planning,
and SQL generation in a single pass ([Pourreza et al.,
2025](#bib.bib34); [Li et al., 2024b](#bib.bib32)). Another prominent
approach involves multi-agent frameworks that improve modularity by
using API calls to closed-source LLMs, where different agent roles are
defined mainly through prompting ([Pourreza et al., 2024](#bib.bib19);
[Liu et al., 2025c](#bib.bib36); [Xie et al., 2025a](#bib.bib10)).

MARS-SQL addresses three main challenges facing SQL agents: (i)
Compositional reasoning: Agents often struggle to formulate and maintain
a coherent long-term plan required for complex queries. For example,
they may fail to correctly combine multiple SQL clauses like joins and
subqueries. This often results in a loop of fixing minor syntax without
ever addressing the flawed high-level logic. ([Chaturvedi et al.,
2025](#bib.bib63)). To tackle this, we introduce a Generation Agent
trained via interactive reinforcement learning, which adopts a
multi-turn reasoning process to decompose complex goals and refine the
query step-by-step. (ii) Schema understanding: Navigating schemas with
massive amounts of irrelevant tables and columns (distractors) is prone
to error. An agent might, for instance, hallucinate columns or
misidentify join keys due to the large search space, leading to
unproductive interactions ([Deng et al., 2025](#bib.bib18)). We address
this via a specialised Grounding Agent that performs reasoning-driven
schema identification, filtering out distractors to provide a precise
schema context for generation. This role separation is especially
helpful when schema grounding and SQL generation would otherwise compete
for the same context budget. (iii) Environmental grounding: While
interactivity is central to agents, current models often lack the
nuanced ability to fully leverage environmental feedback ([Huang et al.,
2025d](#bib.bib72)). They struggle to diagnose specific SQL dialect
errors or recover from ambiguous execution outcomes, limiting their
self-correction capabilities ([Zhang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib13)).
MARS-SQL addresses this via a dual strategy: a Generation Agent that
leverages continuous interaction to decompose complex problems and
execute intermediate queries to guide its reasoning, and a Validation
Agent that executes and verifies the final trajectories against the
environment.

While recent multi-agent frameworks have explored decomposing
Text-to-SQL into modular stages ([Gorti et al., 2025](#bib.bib6); [Liu
et al., 2025c](#bib.bib36)), these approaches primarily rely on static
prompting or supervised fine-tuning of distinct modules. MARS-SQL
distinguishes itself by introducing a novel interactive training
paradigm. Rather than relying on architectural decomposition alone, we
empower the Generation Agent with a multi-turn Reinforcement Learning
(RL) policy trained via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with
sparse execution rewards. This allows the agent to learn how to navigate
the schema and self-correct errors dynamically, rather than merely
following a prompted chain of thought. The core innovation lies in the
Generation Agent’s ability to operate within a ReAct-style
Think-Act-Observe loop ([Yao et al., 2022](#bib.bib30)). As detailed in
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL"),
this process transforms SQL generation into a dynamic investigation. For
instance, when the agent initially attempts to join the hallucinated
“fprm” table, it encounters an OperationalError. Rather than failing
silently, the agent explicitly interprets this feedback, diagnoses the
schema error, and self-corrects to identify the correct “frpm” table. To
further improve robustness, multiple reasoning trajectories are explored
during inference, and the Validation Agent selects the optimal result.
Our deployed system uses three specialized 7B agents, corresponding to
an inference-time footprint of approximately 21B parameters. Through
this synergistic workflow, MARS-SQL achieves strong empirical results,
reaching a new state-of-the-art Execution Accuracy of 77.84% on the BIRD
development set and 89.75% on the Spider test set. Even when compared
through efficiency-oriented analyses under matched latency budgets
(Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F Inference Efficiency and Practicality Analysis ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL")),
MARS-SQL outperforms strictly prompted or self-consistency baselines,
supporting the view that its gains are not explained by added parameters
or inference time alone.

![Refer to caption](2511.01008v2/intro.png)

Figure 1: Illustration of interactive reasoning process.

Our main contributions are as follows:

1.  1.  We introduce MARS-SQL, a trainable multi-agent framework for
        Text-to-SQL. Our contribution is primarily at the workflow level: we
        separate schema grounding, interactive generation, and outcome
        validation, and train these roles instead of relying on a static
        prompted pipeline.
2.  2.  We show how to train an interactive multi-turn generation policy
        with execution feedback. The Generation Agent operates within a
        Think–Act–Observe loop and learns to diagnose errors and
        self-correct from live database feedback, while the Grounding Agent
        further improves schema context management through data-driven
        training.
3.  3.  MARS-SQL achieves strong empirical results, reaching 77.84%
        execution accuracy on BIRD-dev and 89.75% on Spider-test, while also
        generalizing well to additional out-of-domain benchmarks. We further
        show that the gains are not reducible to raw parameter scaling
        alone, and provide an efficiency analysis that characterizes the
        accuracy–latency–memory trade-off of the full framework rather than
        evaluating it only as a single operating point.

## 2 Preliminaries

Background Formulation. The primary goal of a Text-to-SQL system is to
translate a natural language question into an executable SQL query. We
can formally define this task as learning a mapping from a user question
and a group of database schemas to the corresponding SQL query.

![Refer to caption](2511.01008v2/sql_agent0925.png)

Figure 2: The three-stage workflow of MARS-SQL. (1) Grounding: A
Grounding Agent selects the relevant schema. (2) Generation: A
Generation agent produces multiple interaction trajectories using a
Think-Act-Observe loop. (3) Validation: A Validation agent scores and
selects the best trajectory.

Let $`Q`$ be the natural language question posed by a user. Let $`S`$ be
the database schema, which defines the structure of the database. The
schema $`S`$ consists of a set of tables
$`T=\{t_{1},t_{2},\dots,t_{m}\}`$, where each table $`t_{i}`$ is
composed of a set of columns
$`C_{i}=\{c_{i,1},c_{i,2},\dots,c_{i,k}\}`$. The schema also includes
information about data types, primary keys (PKs), and foreign keys (FKs)
that define the relationships between tables. The objective is to
generate a SQL query $`Y`$ such that when it is executed on the database
instance $`D`$, it produces the correct answer to the question $`Q`$.

Conventionally, the Text-to-SQL problem is treated as a
sequence-to-sequence translation task, where the goal is to learn a
function $`f`$: Y = f(Q, S) This formulation, however, treats the
generation as a single, static step and fails to capture the exploratory
and corrective nature required for solving complex analytical queries.

Reformulation as an Interactive Decision Process. As highlighted in the
introduction, the static, one-shot formulation is insufficient for
complex reasoning. A human analyst does not simply translate; they
interact, explore, and refine. To model this more robust process, we
reformulate Text-to-SQL as a sequential decision-making task, grounded
in the ReAct paradigm ([Yao et al., 2023](#bib.bib28)).

Instead of learning a direct mapping to a final query, our goal is to
learn an optimal policy, $`\pi`$, that generates a trajectory of
thoughts and actions to solve the problem. A complete interaction
trajectory, $`\tau`$, is a sequence of multiple rounds:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\tau=(h_{1},\alpha_{1},\omega_{1},\dots,h_{M},\alpha_{M},\omega_{M})
``` |  | (1) |

Each turn in the trajectory consists of:

- •
  Thought ($`h_{t}`$): An internal reasoning step where the agent
  analyzes the problem state, reflects on past observations, and plans
  the next action.
- •
  Action ($`\alpha_{t}`$): An operation chosen by the agent from a
  predefined action space $`\mathcal{A}`$, primarily involving the
  execution of SQL queries against the database.
- •
  Observation ($`\omega_{t}`$): The feedback received from the
  environment after executing action $`\alpha_{t}`$. This could be a
  query result, a database error, or other information that guides the
  agent’s next thought.

Under this formulation, the objective is to learn an optimal policy
$`\pi(\alpha_{t}|Q,S,(h_{<t},\alpha_{<t},\omega_{<t}))`$ that maximizes
the expected total reward over the trajectory, $`E[R(\tau)]`$. The
reward $`R(\tau)`$ is typically determined by the final outcome,
specifically, whether the trajectory successfully produces a correct SQL
query. This interactive, policy-based formulation naturally accommodates
the trial-and-error and self-correction that are essential for tackling
complex, real-world database queries.

## 3 Methodology

As illustrated in Figure
[2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 2 Preliminaries ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL"),
we introduce MARS-SQL, a trainable multi-agent framework that treats
Text-to-SQL generation as an interactive, tool-augmented decision-making
process. Our goal is not to propose a new standalone SQL primitive, but
to make role decomposition and agent–database interaction trainable. The
framework operates in three stages: Grounding, Generation, and
Validation. Initially, a Grounding Agent prunes the full database schema
to only the tables and columns relevant to the user question.
Subsequently, a Generation agent executes a multi-turn rollout,
producing multiple distinct interaction trajectories by actively
querying the database. Finally, a Validation Agent scores each
trajectory, and the one with the highest confidence score is selected as
the final answer.

### 3.1 Grounding Agent: Reasoning-driven Schema Identification

The Grounding Agent performs table-level schema linking. Its goal is to
learn a policy $`\pi_{Ground}`$. For each table
$`t_{i}\in T(1\leq i\leq F)`$ and the user’s question $`Q`$, the agent
takes the pair $`x_{i}=(Q,t_{i})`$ as input. It then generates a
structured output $`o_{i}=(d_{i},C^{\prime}_{i})`$, where
$`d_{i}\in\{\text{`Y', `N'}\}`$ is the relevance decision and
$`C^{\prime}_{i}\subseteq C_{i}`$ is the predicted subset of essential
columns. The final output of this stage is the reduced schema
$`S^{\prime}`$, containing only the tables and columns deemed relevant:
$`S^{\prime}=\{(t_{i},C^{\prime}_{i})\mid o_{i}\text{ has }d_{i}=\text{`Y'}\}`$.

Training Algorithm. We train the agent using Group Relative Policy
Optimization (GRPO) ([Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib43)). For each input
$`x_{i}`$, the model generates a group of $`G`$ candidate outputs
$`\{o_{1},\dots,o_{G}\}`$. The policy $`\pi_{\theta}`$ is then updated
via the objective:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\small\begin{split}J_{\text{GRPO}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}\Bigg[\frac{1}{G}\sum_{j=1}^{G}\min\bigg(\frac{\pi_{\theta}(o_{j}|x_{i})}{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(o_{j}|x_{i})}A_{j},\\
&\hskip-161.87393pt\text{clip}\left(\frac{\pi_{\theta}(o_{j}|x_{i})}{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(o_{j}|x_{i})},1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon\right)A_{j}\bigg)-\beta D_{\text{KL}}(\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{\text{ref}})\Bigg]\end{split}
``` |  | (2) |

where $`A_{j}`$ is the advantage for candidate $`o_{j}`$. The agent’s
prompt template is in
Appendix [26](#A13.T26 "Table 26 ‣ Appendix M Table Level Grounding ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL").

Reward Design. The reward function $`R_{Ground}`$ provides a granular
score based on the accuracy of the agent’s prediction. Let the agent’s
parsed prediction be $`P=(d_{p},C_{p})`$, where
$`d_{p}\in\{\text{`Y', `N'}\}`$ is the relevance decision and $`C_{p}`$
is the set of predicted columns. Let the ground truth be
$`o^{*}=(d_{g},C_{g})`$. The reward $`R_{g}(o,o^{*})`$ is defined as:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
R=\begin{cases}1.0&\text{if }o=o^{*}\\
\max(0.5,\frac{|C_{g}|}{|C_{p}|})&\text{if }d_{p}=d_{g}=\text{`Y'}\text{ and }C_{g}\subset C_{p}\\
0.2&\text{if }d_{p}=\text{`Y'}\text{ and }d_{g}=\text{`N'}\\
0.1&\text{if }d_{p}=d_{g}=\text{`Y'}\text{ and }C_{g}\not\subseteq C_{p}\\
0.0&\text{if response format is invalid}\end{cases}
``` |  |

This heuristic reward shaping is grounded in the principle that missing
schema elements (False Negatives) are fatal, while including extra ones
(False Positives) is merely noisy.

### 3.2 Generation Agent: Multi-turn Trajectory Generation

The Generation Agent is the central component, tasked with producing SQL
queries. Its input is the user question $`Q`$ and the reduced schema
$`S^{\prime}`$ from the Grounding Agent. Its output is a set of $`N`$
candidate interaction trajectories, $`\{\tau_{1},\dots,\tau_{N}\}`$,
where each trajectory comprises of $`M`$ rounds of the Think-Act-Observe
process. The correct trajectory is expected to result in the final SQL
solution $`Y_{i}`$.

MDP Formulation. We model the multi-turn generation process as a Markov
Decision Process (MDP), defined by the tuple
$`(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},P,R)`$.

- •
  State Space $`\mathcal{S}`$: A state $`s_{t}`$ represents the history
  of interaction up to round $`t`$, containing the sequence of past
  thoughts, actions, and observations
  $`((h_{1},\alpha_{1},\omega_{1}),\dots,(h_{t-1},\alpha_{t-1},\omega_{t-1}))`$.
- •
  Action Space $`\mathcal{A}`$: An action $`a_{t}=(h_{t},\alpha_{t})`$
  consists of generating a thought $`h_{t}`$ and an executable SQL
  $`\alpha_{t}`$.
- •
  Transition $`P`$: $`P(s_{t+1}|s_{t},a_{t})`$ is the transition
  probability, which is determined by the environment (i.e., the
  database executing the action $`\alpha_{t}`$).
- •
  Reward $`R`$: The reward function $`R_{gen}(\tau)`$ provides a sparse
  signal based on the final outcome of a complete trajectory $`\tau`$.

The goal is to learn a policy $`\pi_{Gen}(a_{t}|s_{t})`$ that maximizes
the return
$`J(\pi_{Gen})=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\pi_{Gen}}[R_{Gen}(\mathcal{T})]`$.

Training. We train the policy $`\pi_{Gen}`$ using Group Relative Policy
Optimization (GRPO). For an input $`(Q,S^{\prime})`$, we generate a
group of $`G`$ trajectories $`\{\tau_{1},\dots,\tau_{G}\}`$, where each
trajectory $`tau_{i}`$ consists of a sequence of states and actions
$`(s_{0}^{i},a_{0}^{i},s_{1}^{i},\dots)`$. The GRPO objective for
trajectories is defined as formula
[3](#S3.E3 "Equation 3 ‣ 3.2 Generation Agent: Multi-turn Trajectory Generation ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL"),

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |   $`\displaystyle\begin{split}J_{\text{GRPO}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}(Q,S^{\prime})\sim\mathcal{D},\\
\{\tau_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G}\sim\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}\end{subarray}}\Bigg[\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\sum_{t=0}^{|\tau_{i}|-1}\sum_{j=1}^{|a_{t}^{i}|}\min\bigg(\frac{\pi_{\theta}(a_{t,j}^{i}|s_{t}^{i},a_{t,<j}^{i})}{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(a_{t,j}^{i}|s_{t}^{i},a_{t,<j}^{i})}A_{i},\\
&\hskip-265.0004pt\text{clip}\left(\frac{\pi_{\theta}(a_{t,j}^{i}|s_{t}^{i},a_{t,<j}^{i})}{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(a_{t,j}^{i}|s_{t}^{i},a_{t,<j}^{i})},1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon\right)A_{i}\bigg)\Bigg]\end{split}`$ |  | (3) |

where $`a_{t,j}^{i}`$ is the $`j`$-th token of action $`a_{t}^{i}`$ in
trajectory $`\tau_{i}`$, and $`A_{i}`$ is the advantage for the entire
trajectory, computed based on the relative rewards of all trajectories
within the group. The reward signal $`R_{gen}(\tau)`$ used to compute
$`A_{i}`$ is derived solely from execution outcomes, encouraging the
agent to prioritize both syntactic validity and semantic correctness:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
R_{gen}(\tau)=\begin{cases}1.0&\text{if valid and execution correct}\\
0.0&\text{if valid but incorrect}\\
-1.0&\text{if invalid}\end{cases}
``` |  |

This coarse but decisive feedback gives the agent freedom to discover
effective reasoning strategies without being constrained to annotated
step-level traces. Unlike Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) which typically
relies on expensive, human-annotated Chain-of-Thought data, our sparse
reward mechanism allows the agent to learn directly from environmental
feedback. This enables the agent to autonomously discover diverse and
robust error-recovery strategies that are often absent in static
training sets. Consequently, MARS-SQL demonstrates superior data
efficiency, achieving state-of-the-art results with only $`\sim`$35k
training instances, whereas SFT baselines often require millions of
synthetic examples to adequately cover the error space (detaile in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Training Efficiency and Resource Analysis ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL")).

Interactive Reasoning. The agent is grounded in the ReAct paradigm,
interleaving reasoning and acting in a Think-Act-Observe loop. This
iterative structure transforms SQL generation from a one-shot
translation into a dialogue with the database, enabling robust recovery
from errors.

### 3.3 Validation Agent: Verification and Selection

The Validation Agent selects the optimal solution from the multiple
candidates generated. Its input is the set of $`N`$ candidate
trajectories $`\{\tau_{1},\dots,\tau_{N}\}`$ and the original question
$`Q`$. Its output is the single best trajectory,
$`\tau_{\text{final}}`$. We employ a Generative Validation agent $`V`$,
reframing verification as a next-token prediction task that leverages
the base model’s own capabilities.

Training and Inference. The Validation Agent is trained via supervised
fine-tuning (SFT) to generate a single token response: “Yes” for a
correct trajectory or “No” for an incorrect one, conditioned on the
question and trajectory. The prompt structure is in
Appendix [C.1](#A3.SS1 "C.1 Training Dataset ‣ Appendix C Dataset ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL").

At inference time, the agent’s score for a trajectory $`\tau_{i}`$ is
the average probability of the “Yes” token across $`M`$ stochastic
reasoning rounds :

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
V(\tau_{i})=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{j=1}^{M}P(y_{j}=\text{``Yes''}|\tau_{i},Q)
``` |  | (4) |

The trajectory with the highest confidence score is selected as the
final answer. This method effectively turns the generative model into a
high-quality reranker, capable of discerning the most plausible and
accurate reasoning path among many alternatives.

## 4 Experiment

### 4.1 Experiment Setup

Implementations & Efficiency

All agents are based on Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct, implemented in
PyTorch and trained on NVIDIA H800 GPUs. The Grounding and Generation
Agents utilize RL via the Verl ([Sheng et al., 2024](#bib.bib41)) and
SkyRL ([Liu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib42)) frameworks, respectively, while
the Validation Agent is fine-tuned (SFT) on agent-generated
trajectories. For inference, we adopt $`G=8`$ rollouts and $`M=8`$
verification rounds. This is our performance-oriented configuration and
delivers the best overall accuracy. Since the deployed system contains
three specialized 7B agents, we explicitly report both the per-agent
size (7B) and the total inference-time footprint ($`\sim`$21B). We
analyze its latency, token cost, VRAM footprint, normalized-budget
comparisons, and alternative lower-cost operating points in
Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F Inference Efficiency and Practicality Analysis ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL").
The entire multi-agent training pipeline requires only $`\sim`$13 hours
(Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Training Efficiency and Resource Analysis ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL")).
Detailed prompts and hyperparameters are provided in
Appendix [M](#A13 "Appendix M Table Level Grounding ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL"), [H](#A8 "Appendix H Multi-turn Generation ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL")
and [B](#A2 "Appendix B Training Details ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL").

Benchmark Dataset

All experiments are conducted on the BIRD ([Li et al.,
2023](#bib.bib24)), Spider 1.0 ([Yu et al., 2019a](#bib.bib25)) and
Spider-DK ([Gan et al., 2021](#bib.bib23)) datasets. We use BIRD for
in-domain evaluation and Spider and Spider-DK for out-of-domain
evaluation; we further report SParC results in
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Additional Out-of-Domain Robustness ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL").
Dataset details are in
Appendix [C.2](#A3.SS2 "C.2 Evaluation Dataset ‣ Appendix C Dataset ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL").

Table 1: Main results on the BIRD-dev, Spider-test, and Spider-DK
benchmarks. We report Execution Accuracy (%). ‘Thinking?’ indicates
whether the method uses a multi-step reasoning process. For multi-agent
systems, the size column reports the per-agent model size; MARS-SQLuses
three 7B agents ($`\sim`$21B total at inference). Bold indicates the
best result, and underline indicates the second best.

Evaluation Metric

We evaluate model performance using Execution Accuracy (EX), which is
the primary metric for correctness. A predicted SQL query receives a
score of 1 if its execution result is identical to the execution result
of the ground-truth query, and 0 otherwise. The final score is the
percentage of correctly executed queries.

Baseline models

To contextualize the performance of MARS-SQL, we conduct a comprehensive
comparison against a diverse set of models. These are organized into
three distinct categories: Base models, High-performing closed-source
systems, and Trained open-source models.
Base Models: This category includes foundational LLMs used without
task-specific fine-tuning to establish a performance baseline. We
evaluate O3-mini, GPT-4o ([OpenAI, 2023](#bib.bib22)), GPT-5 ([Singh et
al., 2025](#bib.bib7)), Qwen2.5-coder-7B ([Hui et al.,
2024](#bib.bib38)) and Qwen3-coder-30B ([Team, 2025](#bib.bib2)). These
results help gauge the inherent Text-to-SQL capabilities of modern LLMs
before specialized training.
Closed Source Multi agentic framework: This category consists of systems
that leverage powerful proprietary models via APIs, representing the
upper bound of performance achievable with leading commercial
technology. These methods, such as CHESS  ([Talaei et al.,
2024](#bib.bib35)), OpenSearch-SQL  ([Xie et al., 2025c](#bib.bib21)),
XiYan-SQL  ([Liu et al., 2025c](#bib.bib36)), and CHASE-SQL  ([Pourreza
et al., 2024](#bib.bib19)), typically employ sophisticated frameworks
and prompting techniques. This comparison situates our open-source
multi-agent framework performance against industry-leading systems.
Open Source Agentic Framework: This group comprises leading open-source
models specifically fine-tuned for the Text-to-SQL task, representing
the current state-of-the-art in the research community. These models,
including CodeS ([Li et al., 2024b](#bib.bib32)), Share ([Qu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib29)), OmniSQL ([Li et al., 2025a](#bib.bib31)),
Arctic-Text2SQL-R1 ([Yao et al., 2025](#bib.bib33)), and Reasoning
SQL ([Pourreza et al., 2025](#bib.bib34)), employ various advanced
training methodologies. Comparing MARS-SQL against these systems
assesses its competitiveness and advancements over existing specialized
methods.

### 4.2 Main Results

As presented in Table
[1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.1 Experiment Setup ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL"),
our method, MARS-SQL, trained solely on the BIRD training set, achieves
state-of-the-art execution accuracy on both the Bird-dev (77.84%) and
the Spider-test (89.75%). Additionally, it obtains the second-highest
score on the Spider-DK benchmark with 78.13%.

In-Domain Performance on BIRD-dev.

On the in-domain BIRD-dev set, MARS-SQL establishes a new
state-of-the-art with an execution accuracy of 77.84%. This result
represents a significant improvement of 5.55% over the next best
open-source competitor, Reasoning SQL (72.29%). More impressively, our
system outperforms all listed closed-source solutions, including the
strong CHASE-SQL + Gemini (74.90%). This demonstrates the superior
effectiveness of our training methodology on this complex, real-world
benchmark.

| Configuration | Agent Size | \# agents | Bird dev (%) | Spider test (%) | Spider DK (%) |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Generator Only (Base) | 7B | 1 | 66.37 | 80.11 | 69.91 |
| w/o verifier (Grounder+ RL Generator) | 7B | 2 | 68.71 | 80.72 | 70.65 |
| w/o Grounder (RL Generator + Verifier) | 7B | 2 | 69.75 | 89.19 | 77.01 |
| w/ Self-Consistency (instead of Verifier) | 7B | 2 | 72.93 | 83.51 | 73.08 |
| MARS-SQL (Full Framework) | 7B | 3 | 77.84 | 89.75 | 78.13 |

Table 2: Ablation study on the components of our multi-agent framework.
We evaluate the contribution of each agent (Grounder, Verifier). The
final row, MARS-SQL, represents our full proposed model.

![Refer to caption](2511.01008v2/performance.png)

Figure 3: Execution accuracy on Bird-dev of models fine-tuned with
different maximum interaction turns (T), evaluated at inference turn
limits of 1, 5, and 10. ‘Greedy’ uses a single generation trajectory
($`N=1`$) without validation; ‘Selected’ denotes the final trajectory
chosen by the Validation Agent from $`N=8`$ candidates; and ‘Best of N’
represents the oracle upper bound where the question is considered
correct if any of the $`N`$ candidates matches.

Out-of-Domain Generalization.

The out-of-domain generalization of MARS-SQL is particularly noteworthy,
demonstrated by its strong performance on both the Spider-test and
Spider-DK benchmarks. On the broad Spider-test set, it achieves a
state-of-the-art score of 89.75%, showcasing exceptional generalization
to unseen schemas and question types. This robustness extends to the
specialized Spider-DK benchmark, which tests for implicit domain
knowledge, where MARS-SQLsecures a competitive second-highest score of
78.13%. Crucially, these results were achieved without any exposure to
the Spider training set. This contrasts with competitors like
Arctic-Text2SQL-R1, which required training on Spider data (from which
Spider-DK is derived) to achieve its high scores. We further include
additional out-of-domain evidence on SParC in
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Additional Out-of-Domain Robustness ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL").
Together, these results highlight that training solely on the diverse
BIRD dataset effectively equips the model for broad cross-domain and
interaction-heavy challenges.

### 4.3 Ablation Studies

Multi-agent frame components analysis.

We conduct a systematic ablation study to validate the contribution of
each key component in our MARS-SQL framework, with results presented in
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL").
The analysis confirms that both the Schema Grounder and the Generative
Validation Agent are useful components, though their impact is not
uniform across datasets. The Validation Agent provides the most
consistent gain: our purpose-built verifier substantially outperforms a
strong alternative like Self-Consistency (77.84% vs. 72.93% on
BIRD-dev), highlighting the benefits of specialized validation. The
Grounder is especially helpful on BIRD-dev and more modest on
Spider-test, which is consistent with our later analysis that grounding
matters most under larger, noisier, or more ambiguous schemas. We
therefore view the framework’s gain as arising from complementary roles
rather than from every component contributing equally in every setting.
This interpretation is further reinforced by single-model multi-task
baselines: when a single Qwen2.5-Coder model is SFT-trained to perform
grounding, generation, and validation within one shared model, 14B and
32B variants reach only 55.67% and 57.82% EX on BIRD-dev, respectively
(Appendix [G](#A7 "Appendix G Architecture versus Parameter Scaling ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL")).

Controlled isolation of component gains.

To better separate the effects of structured inference, learned
interaction, and reranking, we further conduct a dataset-wide
controlled-isolation analysis on BIRD-dev. Starting from a strict
baseline consisting of the RL Generator only with $`T{=}1`$ and greedy
decoding, we add exactly one mechanism at a time using configurations
already studied in our manuscript. The results are summarized in
Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.3 Ablation Studies ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL"),
with further details in
Appendix [J](#A10 "Appendix J Dataset-Wide Controlled Isolation ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL").

| Mechanism                | Extra Solved | Gain    |
|--------------------------|--------------|---------|
| Schema pruning           | 56           | +3.63%  |
| RL interactive reasoning | 44           | +2.89%  |
| Generative verification  | 131          | +8.54%  |
| Total improvement        | 231          | +15.06% |

Table 3: Dataset-wide controlled isolation on BIRD-dev. We report the
additional queries resolved beyond the strict RL-Generator baseline
(62.78% EX).

This analysis sharpens the causal picture in two ways. First, the
largest isolated gain comes from generative verification, which is
consistent with our ablations and selection-method comparisons. Second,
the RL interactive policy still contributes 44 additional correct
queries under greedy decoding alone, without relying on sampling or
reranking. This provides direct evidence that execution-feedback-driven
interaction improves the underlying policy itself rather than only
helping through best-of-$`N`$ selection.

Influence of different max interaction turns.

We then study the impact of the maximum interaction turns (T) during
Reinforcement Learning. The results are visualized in
Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL"),
with full details provided in
Appendix [K](#A11 "Appendix K Interaction turns impact ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL").
As shown, increasing T from 1 to 10 consistently improves both Greedy
and Best of 8 accuracy. Notably, our model trained with T=10
significantly outperforms models trained with fewer turns across all
inference settings. For instance, at Inference (T=10), it achieves
69.88% Greedy accuracy, surpassing the T=1 model (67.60%) and the base
model (55.76%). Furthermore, this process enhances single-pass
reliability by narrowing the gap between Best of 8 (potential) and
Greedy (actual) performance. This gap shrinks from a substantial 23.33%
in the base model to 12.19% in the T=1 model at Inference (T=1).
Training with a larger T reinforces this effect, making the model’s
greedy output more aligned with its optimal potential, thereby improving
its dependability. Beyond accuracy, RL also improves interaction
efficiency: the trained Generation Agent uses fewer average interaction
turns than the base model across difficulty levels, while still
retaining the ability to spend more turns on long-tail difficult cases.
We report this rollout-length evolution and turn distribution in
Appendix [H](#A8 "Appendix H Multi-turn Generation ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL"),
Table [21](#A8.T21 "Table 21 ‣ Appendix H Multi-turn Generation ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL"),
and
Table [22](#A8.T22 "Table 22 ‣ Appendix H Multi-turn Generation ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL").

![Refer to caption](2511.01008v2/verifier_compare_new.png)

Figure 4: Comparison of different selection strategies.

Selection methods analysis.

To validate the effectiveness of our Generative Validation Agent, we
compare it against several alternative selection strategies, as
illustrated in
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.3 Ablation Studies ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL").
While common approaches such as Self-Consistency or using a powerful LLM
as a Judge (e.g., GPT-4.1) provide a reasonable baseline, their
performance is suboptimal and inconsistent across the different
benchmarks. In contrast, our fine-tuned Generative Validation Agent
consistently outperforms all other methods by a significant margin. On
the challenging Spider-test, it achieves a correct selection rate of
97.15%, a substantial improvement over the next-best strategy’s 92.09%.
Similar significant gains are observed on both BIRD-dev and Spider-DK.
This consistent superiority demonstrates the stability and robustness of
our specialized approach. Unlike general-purpose models or
heuristic-based methods, our Validation Agent reliably identifies the
most accurate reasoning trajectory, making it a critical component for
achieving state-of-the-art performance. Full execution accuracy results
are detailed in
Appendix [Q](#A17 "Appendix Q Selection method comparison ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL").

## 5 Related Work

LLMs for Text-to-SQL

The rise of Large Language Models (LLMs) has brought notable progress to
Text-to-SQL tasks, moving past traditional sequence-to-sequence
approaches. Recent studies emphasize in-context learning, where
strategies such as Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting are used to break
down complex queries into intermediate reasoning steps ([Tai et al.,
2023](#bib.bib14); [Dong et al., 2023](#bib.bib15)). Frameworks like
DIN-SQL ([Pourreza and Rafiei, 2023](#bib.bib16)) and DAIL-SQL ([Gao et
al., 2023](#bib.bib26)) have systematically explored prompt engineering
and multi-stage pipelines that include schema linking, generation, and
refinement to boost performance. Building on these ideas, more recent
studies  ([Wang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib17); [Deng et al.,
2025](#bib.bib18); [Gao et al., 2025](#bib.bib20); [Xie et al.,
2025c](#bib.bib21); [Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib5)) move toward
structured, multi-step workflows that better match the complexity of
real databases and diverse queries. Notably, while works like
MSc-SQL ([Gorti et al., 2025](#bib.bib6)) employ multi-sample critiquing
via supervised fine-tuning, our work shifts away from fixed datasets or
static prompting by introducing a dynamic, reinforcement-learning-based
agentic system that optimizes interaction trajectories directly against
execution feedback.

Multi-Agent systems

Large Language Models (LLMs) have enabled sophisticated multi-agent
systems by adopting specialized roles via in-context prompting ([Wang et
al., 2024](#bib.bib44); [Min et al., 2022](#bib.bib45)). Our focus is on
goal-oriented problem-solving frameworks, rather than social
simulations ([Zhang et al., 2024](#bib.bib54); [Hua et al.,
2024](#bib.bib55); [Yuan et al., 2023](#bib.bib40)), where tasks are
divided among collaborating agents. The complexity of these
collaborations has grown from simple debating ([Du et al.,
2023](#bib.bib51)) to structured workflows with the use of tools, such
as software development agents ChatDev ([Qian et al.,
2024](#bib.bib52)), MedTutor-R1  ([He et al., 2025b](#bib.bib37)) and
CollabUIAgent ([He et al., 2025a](#bib.bib71)). Other notable approaches
include the generic framework AutoGen ([Wu et al., 2023](#bib.bib50))
and the dynamic cooperation in AutoAgents ([Chen et al.,
2024](#bib.bib53)). Following this established paradigm, we propose a
specialized pipeline for Text-to-SQL using Grounding, Generation, and
Validation agents.

Reinforcement Learning

Reinforcement Learning (RL) is increasingly used to enhance the complex
reasoning capabilities of LLMs, especially when combined with
chain-of-thought prompting  ([Wei et al., 2023](#bib.bib47); [OpenAI,
2024](#bib.bib46); [Su et al., 2025](#bib.bib9)). This approach has
proven highly effective, achieving state-of-the-art results in fields
like mathematics and code generation ([Qin et al., 2023](#bib.bib56);
[Zhao et al., 2024](#bib.bib57)). Typical approaches fine-tune models
with policy gradient methods such as PPO or GRPO, rewarding logical
soundness or correct outcomes  ([Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib43);
[DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025](#bib.bib48); [Huang et al.,
2025c](#bib.bib8); [He et al., 2025b](#bib.bib37)). While PPO is a
common choice, GRPO offers advantages by being less prone to high
variance and more memory-efficient, as it does not require loading an
additional critic model. In parallel, interactive reasoning paradigms
like ReAct ([Yao et al., 2022](#bib.bib30)) leverage prompting-based
Think–Act–Observe loops to enable tool use and self-correction, but
without explicit policy training. While Text-to-SQL requires similarly
complex reasoning, explicit RL for this domain remains underexplored.
Our work addresses this gap by training the Generation agent’s policy
with execution-based rewards, enabling robust, stateful query generation
and dynamic self-correction.

Test-Time Scaling

To enhance performance without the cost of retraining, many researchers
have focused on inference-time techniques. Self-consistency, for
instance, has become a popular method where multiple reasoning paths are
sampled and the final answer is chosen by majority vote ([Wang et al.,
2023](#bib.bib58)). This concept has been further refined by
verification and reranking methods, which employ an external mechanism
or model to score and select the best candidate from a pool of
outputs ([Zheng et al., 2023](#bib.bib59); [Gu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib60)). Our approach builds on the recent innovation of
Generative Verifiers ([Zhang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib61)). Instead of a
voting process or a separate classifier, our Validation Agent reframes
selection as a next-token prediction problem. It assesses each potential
solution trajectory by calculating the probability of the model
generating a “Yes” token, ultimately selecting the trajectory with the
highest confidence score.

## 6 Conclusion

In this work, we introduced MARS-SQL, the first framework to leverage an
interactive RL policy for tool-augmented SQL generation under sparse
execution rewards within a multi-agent decomposition. Unlike static,
single-pass approaches, our method uniquely couples this dynamic
generation policy, which learns to reason and self-correct via a
ReAct-style loop, with a generative probability-based trajectory
selection mechanism tailored for SQL verification. This unified
methodology enables MARS-SQL to establish new state-of-the-art execution
accuracies on BIRD (77.84%) and Spider (89.75%), demonstrating
exceptional cross-domain generalization by achieving top-tier
performance on Spider without any in-domain training. Our ablation
studies confirm the criticality of this synergistic design, suggesting
that shifting from prompt engineering to interactive, policy-driven
reasoning is a pivotal direction for building dependable, data-centric
AI systems.

At the same time, we emphasize an important practical limitation.
Although each module is 7B-scale, the deployed system contains three
specialized agents and therefore has an inference-time footprint of
approximately 21B parameters. This introduces a real trade-off between
multi-agent specialization and single-model scaling. Our new analyses
show that the observed accuracy gains are not explained by parameter
count alone, but the deployment cost of the full pipeline remains higher
than that of a single 7B model. We therefore view transparent reporting
of total parameters, latency, token usage, and VRAM as essential for
future work on efficient Text-to-SQL agents.

## Impact Statement

This paper introduces MARS-SQL, a multi-agent framework designed to
advance the field of Machine Learning by enabling more robust and
self-correcting autonomous agents in complex data environments. By
reframing Text-to-SQL as an interactive decision-making process grounded
in reinforcement learning, our work significantly lowers the technical
barriers for non-expert users to interact with large-scale, professional
databases, thereby fostering the democratization of data-driven insights
across diverse sectors. The specialized roles of grounding, generation,
and validation agents directly address the critical societal need for
more dependable AI systems, specifically by mitigating common risks such
as model hallucinations and the propagation of incorrect query results
in real-world applications. While this technology empowers individuals
to perform complex data analysis without advanced programming knowledge,
it also emphasizes a move toward transparent and verifiable AI,
encouraging a deployment model that balances automation with
human-in-the-loop oversight to ensure the ethical and responsible use of
generated information.

## Appendix A The Use of Large Language Models

Large Language Models (LLMs) were utilized in a limited, assistive
capacity for specific tasks in this project. For manuscript preparation,
the authors supplied their own draft to an LLM, which then provided
suggestions to improve grammar, enhance clarity, and ensure an academic
tone. The LLM was also used to generate a list of potential titles for
inspiration, though the final title was conceived and refined by the
authors and not taken directly from any single output. In the
implementation phase, an LLM served as a coding assistant by offering
code completions and debugging support. However, all final code,
experimental design, and validation were implemented and verified
exclusively by the authors. It is important to emphasize that LLMs were
NOT used for core scientific contributions, such as generating research
ideas, designing experiments, or conducting the literature review. All
conceptual work and experimental design originated solely with the
authors.

## Appendix B Training Details

This section provides the detailed hyperparameters used for training our
three agents. All agents were trained on NVIDIA H800 GPUs.

### B.1 Grounding Agent

The Grounding Agent was trained using Reinforcement Learning baesd on
Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct. Its primary role is to identify the correct
database schema entities relevant to the user’s question. The training
was conducted using the Verl framework ([Sheng et al.,
2024](#bib.bib41)). The hyperparameters for the RL training and data
generation phases are detailed in
Table [4](#A2.T4 "Table 4 ‣ B.2 Generation Agent ‣ Appendix B Training Details ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL").

Training Steps and Convergence: We trained the Grounding Agent for 600
steps with a batch size of 64. During training, we observed clear
stability and convergence patterns in the reward curves; the reward
consistently increased and then plateaued, indicating that the policy
was successfully optimized.

### B.2 Generation Agent

The Generation Agent was also trained using Reinforcement Learning based
on Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct, leveraging a training framework adapted
from SkyRL ([Liu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib42)). This agent is responsible
for generating the reasoning SQL query trajectories. Its training and
data generation hyperparameters are identical to those of the Grounding
Agent, as shown in
Table [4](#A2.T4 "Table 4 ‣ B.2 Generation Agent ‣ Appendix B Training Details ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL").

Training Steps and Convergence: This agent was trained for 160 steps
with a batch size of 64. Similar to the Grounding Agent, the reward
curve demonstrated stable convergence within this efficient training
phase.

Table 4: Hyperparameters for Grounding and Generation Agent RL Training.

|                               |                     |
|-------------------------------|---------------------|
| Parameter                     | Value               |
| Training Parameters           |                     |
| Learning Rate                 | $`1\times 10^{-6}`$ |
| Batch Size                    | 128                 |
| Trajectory Rollout Parameters |                     |
| Temperature                   | 0.6                 |
| Top-p                         | 0.95                |

Table 5: Hyperparameters for Validation Agent Dataset Generation.

| Parameter               | Value |
|-------------------------|-------|
| Candidates per Question | 16    |
| Temperature             | 0.7   |
| Top-p                   | 0.9   |
| Top-k                   | 50    |

### B.3 Validation Agent

The Validation Agent was trained via Supervised Fine-tuning (SFT) to
select the best SQL query from the candidates generated by the
Generation Agent. We performed a full-parameter fine-tuning of the
Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct model ([Hui et al., 2024](#bib.bib38)) using
the Llama Factory framework. The SFT training hyperparameters are listed
in
Table [6](#A2.T6 "Table 6 ‣ B.3 Validation Agent ‣ Appendix B Training Details ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL"),
and the parameters for generating its training dataset are in
Table [5](#A2.T5 "Table 5 ‣ B.2 Generation Agent ‣ Appendix B Training Details ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL").

|--------------------------|---------------------------|
| Parameter                | Value                     |
| Base Model               | Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct |
````
