## Appendix C Dataset

### C.1 Training Dataset

Our training data is derived from the Bird benchmark, which comprises
9,428 question-SQL pairs. To ensure high quality, we first filtered this
dataset by removing samples flagged as incorrect  ([Pourreza et al.,
2025](#bib.bib34); [Li et al., 2024b](#bib.bib32)) by both
Gemini-2.5-pro and GPT-4o, resulting in a clean set of 8,036 training
examples. From this set, we constructed the fine-tuning data for the
grounding task. For each of the 8,036 question-database pairs, we
generated a distinct training instance for every table within that
database. This process resulted in a large-scale dataset of 90,102
individual data points. For each point, the ground truth—whether a table
is relevant and which of its columns are used—was programmatically
extracted from the gold SQL query using the SQLGlot parser.

We constructed a specialized dataset for training the Verifier via
Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT). First, for each question in our filtered
BIRD training set, we used both our fine-tuned Generator agent and the
initial base model to perform inference, generating a diverse pool of 16
candidate trajectories per question. This ensures the Validation Agent
is exposed to a wide range of reasoning paths, both correct and flawed.
From this pool, we curated a preference dataset by selecting one
positive example (a trajectory leading to a correct execution result)
and one negative example (a trajectory leading to an incorrect result)
for each question. We mix the order of correct and incorrect
trajectories in each pair at random to prevent order bias during
training. Since the number of cases containing both correct and
incorrect trajectories is limited, some questions yield only flawed
trajectories. In such cases, we add the ground truth SQL query in the
prompt as a suggestion to help the model generate proper trajectories.
We applied best-of-N and worst-of-N ([Gui et al., 2024](#bib.bib66))
strategies to select both positive and negative examples. This process
yielded a final dataset of approximately 16,000 training instances. Each
instance is a triplet containing the user’s question, the full
interaction trajectory (including all \[Think\], \[SQL\], and
\[Observation\] steps), and the final execution result.

### C.2 Evaluation Dataset

BIRD is a large-scale, realistic benchmark designed to evaluate modern
Text-to-SQL systems. It features complex databases (33.4 GB across 95
databases), questions from 37 professional domains, and imperfect
real-world data values requiring robust handling. BIRD uniquely
emphasizes the generation of both correct and efficient SQL queries,
making it an ideal testbed for our framework. Our primary evaluations
are performed on its development set, which contains 1,534 examples.

Spider 1.0 is a comprehensive, cross-domain benchmark containing 10,181
questions and 5,693 unique complex SQL queries across 200 multi-table
databases. It serves as a standard for evaluating cross-domain
Text-to-SQL performance. For our evaluation, we use the official test
set, which includes 2,147 examples.

Spider-DK, an extension of Spider, is designed specifically to test a
model’s ability to handle queries requiring implicit domain knowledge.
It comprises samples from the Spider development set that were manually
modified to depend on real-world information for correct interpretation.
This benchmark simulates scenarios where user queries rely on specific
domain context. We evaluate our model on the Spider-DK test set, which
contains 535 examples.

SParC ([Yu et al., 2019b](#bib.bib4)) is a conversational and
cross-domain Text-to-SQL benchmark in which each user question depends
on the preceding interaction context. We use it as an additional
robustness check because it stresses both cross-domain transfer and
multi-turn understanding.

## Appendix D Additional Out-of-Domain Robustness

To complement the main-paper results on Spider-test and Spider-DK, we
further evaluate MARS-SQL on SParC.
Table [7](#A4.T7 "Table 7 ‣ Appendix D Additional Out-of-Domain Robustness ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL")
shows that our model remains strong across these out-of-domain settings,
including a particularly large gain on SParC, a benchmark that stresses
contextual and interaction-heavy reasoning.

| Model           | Spider-test | Spider-DK | SParC |
|-----------------|-------------|-----------|-------|
| GPT-O3-mini     | 78.82       | 71.77     | 67.0  |
| GPT-5           | 77.10       | 66.92     | 61.8  |
| Qwen2.5-7B      | 75.87       | 61.31     | 64.1  |
| MARS-SQL (Ours) | 89.75       | 78.13     | 85.78 |

Table 7: Additional out-of-domain robustness results. All numbers are
execution accuracy (%).

## Appendix E Training Efficiency and Resource Analysis

To address concerns regarding the computational resources required for
our multi-agent framework, we provide a detailed breakdown of the
training time and a comparative analysis of data efficiency. All
experiments were conducted on a node equipped with 4 $`\times`$ NVIDIA
H800 GPUs.

### E.1 Computational Cost Breakdown

Contrary to the perception that training multiple agents is
prohibitively resource-intensive, our framework is designed for rapid
convergence. As detailed in
Table [8](#A5.T8 "Table 8 ‣ E.1 Computational Cost Breakdown ‣ Appendix E Training Efficiency and Resource Analysis ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL"),
the entire specialized training pipeline—including the SFT for the
Validation Agent and GRPO-based Reinforcement Learning for both the
Grounding and Generation Agents—completes in approximately 13 hours.
This represents a modest one-time computational cost, especially
considering the significant performance gains achieved.

| Agent            | Method | Training Steps | Batch Size | Est. Training Time |
|------------------|--------|----------------|------------|--------------------|
| Validation Agent | SFT    | $`\sim`$10k    | 4          | 1 h                |
| Grounding Agent  | GRPO   | 600            | 64         | 4 h                |
| Generation Agent | GRPO   | 160            | 64         | 8 h                |
| Total            |        |                |            | $`\sim`$13 h       |

Table 8: One-Time Training Cost breakdown on 4 $`\times`$ NVIDIA H800
GPUs.

### E.2 Data Efficiency and Comparative Analysis

The efficiency of MARS-SQL stems from its ability to learn diverse
reasoning and self-correction behaviors through interaction and
self-play, rather than relying on massive-scale supervised datasets.

Table [9](#A5.T9 "Table 9 ‣ E.2 Data Efficiency and Comparative Analysis ‣ Appendix E Training Efficiency and Resource Analysis ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL")
compares our framework against standard single-agent SFT approaches.
While standard SFT on the BIRD training set (12k examples) takes only  2
hours, it yields a significantly lower execution accuracy (EX) of
61.08%. Scaling up SFT, as seen in methods like OminiSQL (utilizing 2.5M
examples), requires approximately 20 days of training yet only reaches
64.50% EX.

In contrast, MARS-SQL achieves a state-of-the-art EX of 77.84% using
only 35k LLM-labeled examples and 13 hours of training. To match this
performance level using a single-agent SFT-only paradigm, we
conservatively estimate—based on scaling laws—that it would require
approximately 15 million synthetic examples and 3–4 months of training
time on the same hardware. Thus, our multi-agent RL framework offers
orders of magnitude better data and compute efficiency.

| Method | Annotation Source | Data Size | Training Time (wall) | Dev EX (%) |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| Original (Baseline) | — | — | — | 54.56 |
| SFT on BIRD-train | Human | 12,000 | $`\sim`$2 h | 61.08 |
| Large SFT (e.g., OminiSQL) | LLM + Human | 2,500,000 | $`\sim`$20 days | 64.50 |
| MARS-SQL (Ours) | LLM | 35,000 | $`\sim`$13 h | 77.84 |

Table 9: Cost and efficiency analysis compared with single-agent SFT
baselines on Bird-Dev.

## Appendix F Inference Efficiency and Practicality Analysis

In this section, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the efficiency
and practicality of the MARS-SQL framework. Our goal is not to argue
that all systems should be compared as if they had identical product
characteristics. Instead, we characterize the end-to-end cost of
MARS-SQL and analyze whether its additional test-time compute translates
into meaningful accuracy gains compared with both Text-to-SQL baselines
and general reasoning models. Since MARS-SQL is deployed as three
specialized 7B agents, we additionally report the total inference-time
parameter footprint ($`\sim`$21B) and the practical VRAM implications of
sequential versus fully online deployment. Our analysis covers five
aspects: (1) baseline latency and token cost, (2) memory footprint, (3)
performance under normalized time budgets, (4) adjustable cost–accuracy
trade-offs, and (5) potential system-level optimizations.

### F.1 Baseline Time and Token Cost Analysis

We first present the latency breakdown for our standard SOTA-performing
configuration ($`N_{g}=8`$ trajectories, $`N_{v}=8`$ validation
samples). As shown in
Table [10](#A6.T10 "Table 10 ‣ F.1 Baseline Time and Token Cost Analysis ‣ Appendix F Inference Efficiency and Practicality Analysis ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL"),
the average end-to-end latency is 22.12 seconds per query to achieve
77.84% accuracy.

| Stage | Avg. Time (s) | Description |
|----|----|----|
| 1. Grounding Agent | 0.78s | Aggregated calls (1 per table) |
| 2. Generation Agent | 18.77s | Generating $`N_{g}=8`$ trajectories |
| 3. Validation Agent | 2.58s | Validating $`N_{g}=8`$ trajectories ($`N_{v}=8`$ samples each) |
| Ref: SQL Exec Time | (2.37s) | Avg. time to execute the ground truth SQL |
| Total (End-to-End) | 22.12s | Sum of all stages |

Table 10: Average End-to-End Latency Analysis of MARS-SQL on the BIRD
dev set (Hardware: 1x A6000, num_cpus=32). Times represent the average
latency to generate one SQL query.

The token consumption is analyzed in
Table [11](#A6.T11 "Table 11 ‣ F.1 Baseline Time and Token Cost Analysis ‣ Appendix F Inference Efficiency and Practicality Analysis ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL").
The Generation Agent, utilizing a multi-turn “Think-Act-Observe” loop,
accounts for the majority of the token usage.

| Stage | Avg. Tokens | Description |
|----|----|----|
| 1. Grounding Agent | 875 | Prompt + Schema + Question + Output |
| 2. Generation Agent | 9,200 | $`N_{g}=8\times`$ (Prompt + Schema + Question + Traj.) |
| 3. Validation Agent | 3,250 | $`N_{g}=8\times N_{v}=8\times`$ (Prompt + Trajectory) |
| Total (Avg.) | 13,325 | Sum of all components |

Table 11: Average Token Cost Analysis per Query.

### F.2 Memory Footprint and Deployment Implications

The latency and token analyses above do not fully characterize
deployment cost, because MARS-SQL is a three-agent system. We therefore
report the memory footprint of the full pipeline under a
HuggingFace-based sequential deployment that avoids additional
engine-level pre-allocation. In this setup, the three agents are
executed sequentially (Grounder $`\rightarrow`$ Generator
$`\rightarrow`$ Validation), so the peak VRAM is close to that of a
single active 7B agent rather than the sum of all three models loaded
simultaneously.

| Deployment Setting | VRAM | Note |
|----|----|----|
| Single 7B checkpoint (BF16 weights on disk) | 15.22 GB | Static checkpoint size |
| Sequential inference peak (2K context) | $`\approx`$18.5 GB | One active agent at a time |
| Estimated full online deployment (3 agents resident) | $`\approx`$46 GB | Sum of weights + runtime buffers |
| A6000 + SGLang (observed) | $`\approx`$41 GB | Includes engine pre-allocation |
| A6000 + vLLM (observed) | $`\approx`$47 GB | Includes engine pre-allocation |

Table 12: VRAM footprint of MARS-SQL under different deployment
assumptions.

This distinction matters for interpreting the “7B-class” description.
Each module is indeed built from a 7B model, but the total
inference-time system footprint is approximately 21B parameters. At the
same time, peak VRAM in our default sequential execution is much closer
to a single 7B deployment than to loading all three modules
simultaneously. In other words, parameter count and peak memory are
related but not identical metrics in our setting.

We also emphasize that the higher VRAM observed with SGLang or vLLM on
A6000 GPUs reflects system-level optimization choices such as memory
reservation and kernel/workspace pre-allocation for throughput, rather
than the intrinsic minimum memory required by the model weights
themselves.

### F.3 Accuracy–Latency Trade-offs

We next analyze whether the additional latency of MARS-SQL translates
into meaningful performance gains. Our GPT-5.2 comparison is *not*
intended as a direct system-level comparison with MARS-SQL. Instead, it
is used to illustrate the efficiency of test-time compute trade-offs
within a similar model family: additional “thinking” time is valuable
when it yields sufficiently large accuracy gains.
Table [13](#A6.T13 "Table 13 ‣ F.3 Accuracy–Latency Trade-offs ‣ Appendix F Inference Efficiency and Practicality Analysis ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL")
summarizes this comparison under a unified local profiling setup, while
Figure [5](#A6.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ F.3 Accuracy–Latency Trade-offs ‣ Appendix F Inference Efficiency and Practicality Analysis ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL")
visualizes the same trend as an accuracy–latency frontier. From this
perspective, MARS-SQL follows the same principle but delivers a stronger
return on added latency for Text-to-SQL. To further address the concern
that a strong single-agent baseline might catch up given a comparable
inference budget, we also evaluate a high-budget SQL-R1 setting with 64
sampled outputs and majority voting.

| Method                       | Total Time (s) | EX Acc. (%) |
|------------------------------|----------------|-------------|
| GPT-5.2-instant              | 6.0            | 65.8        |
| GPT-5.2-thinking             | 15.0           | 68.6        |
| SQL-R1                       | 6.5            | 66.43       |
| SQL-R1 + 64 Samples + Voting | 33.8           | 67.34       |
| MARS-SQL (Ours)              | 22.1           | 77.8        |

Table 13: Accuracy–latency trade-off under a unified local profiling
setup. “Total Time” includes generation and SQL execution.

This interpretation is further supported by the incremental
accuracy-per-second return of extra test-time compute. GPT-5.2-instant
$`\rightarrow`$ GPT-5.2-thinking yields approximately $`+0.31`$ acc/sec,
while SQL-R1 $`\rightarrow`$ MARS-SQL yields approximately $`+0.73`$
acc/sec. Importantly, even when SQL-R1 is given a substantially larger
test-time budget than MARS-SQL (33.8s vs. 22.1s), its final
majority-voted accuracy remains only 67.34%. In other words, MARS-SQL
does not simply spend more time; it converts additional latency into
larger execution-accuracy gains on challenging Text-to-SQL reasoning,
which is also visible in
Figure [5](#A6.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ F.3 Accuracy–Latency Trade-offs ‣ Appendix F Inference Efficiency and Practicality Analysis ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL").

![Refer to caption](2511.01008v2/figures/pareto.png)

Figure 5: Accuracy–latency Pareto plot using the methods shown in
Table [13](#A6.T13 "Table 13 ‣ F.3 Accuracy–Latency Trade-offs ‣ Appendix F Inference Efficiency and Practicality Analysis ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL").
MARS-SQL lies on the high-accuracy frontier and extends the same trend
observed in reasoning models: more test-time compute can be worthwhile
when it buys substantially better execution accuracy.

To further separate this observation from any product-level benefits
unique to proprietary systems,
Table [14](#A6.T14 "Table 14 ‣ F.3 Accuracy–Latency Trade-offs ‣ Appendix F Inference Efficiency and Practicality Analysis ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL")
reports the same style of comparison on open-weight reasoning models.
Across Qwen3-30B-A3B, gpt-oss-20B, and GPT-5.2, enabling more
deliberative inference consistently trades latency for higher accuracy.
MARS-SQL occupies the high-accuracy end of the same trend, and also
shows the highest accuracy gain per added second among the comparisons
reported here.

| Method | Time (s) | Acc. (%) | Note |
|----|----|----|----|
| Qwen3-30B-A3B (No Thinking) | 1.3 | 48.11 | — |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B (With Thinking) | 15.8 | 54.69 | +6.58% ACC for +14.5s |
| gpt-oss-20B (No Thinking) | 3.6 | 52.74 | — |
| gpt-oss-20B (With Thinking) | 12.4 | 55.80 | +3.06% ACC for +8.8s |
| GPT-5.2-instant (No Thinking) | 6.0 | 65.8 | — |
| GPT-5.2-thinking (With Thinking) | 15.0 | 68.6 | +2.8% ACC for +9.0s |
| SQL-R1 | 6.5 | 66.43 | — |
| SQL-R1 + 64 Samples + Voting | 33.8 | 67.34 | +0.91% ACC for +27.3s |
| MARS-SQL (Ours) | 22.1 | 77.8 | +11.4% ACC for +15.6s vs. SQL-R1 |

Table 14: Open-weight and reasoning-model comparisons under the same
profiling setup.

### F.4 Performance Comparison Under Normalized Time Budget

The accuracy–latency curves above compare several operating regimes, but
one reviewer-facing concern is even more direct: can a strong
single-agent system match MARS-SQL if it is granted the same wall-clock
budget? To answer this, we additionally compare against self-consistency
baselines under an equal time budget of approximately 22 seconds,
matching the standard MARS-SQL configuration ($`N_{g}=8,N_{v}=8`$). The
SFT baseline uses the budget to generate 16 independent samples, while
the closed-source baseline uses the budget to make four independent API
calls; both select the final answer by self-consistency.

| Method                      | Configuration    | Avg. Latency     | EX Acc. (%) |
|-----------------------------|------------------|------------------|-------------|
| Qwen-SFT (Self-Consistency) | SFT + 16 samples | $`\approx`$22.0s | 64.2        |
| GPT-5 (Self-Consistency)    | 4 API calls      | $`\approx`$22.0s | 69.3        |
| MARS-SQL (Ours)             | Multi-agent RL   | 22.12s           | 77.84       |

Table 15: Accuracy comparison under a normalized time budget
($`\approx`$22s).

As shown in
Table [15](#A6.T15 "Table 15 ‣ F.4 Performance Comparison Under Normalized Time Budget ‣ Appendix F Inference Efficiency and Practicality Analysis ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL"),
these baselines fail to match the performance of MARS-SQL even when
granted an equivalent time budget. This supports the view that the gain
comes from the structured multi-agent reasoning workflow and trained
trajectory validation, rather than merely from spending more inference
time.

### F.5 Adjustable Cost–Accuracy Trade-offs

The latency reported in
Table [10](#A6.T10 "Table 10 ‣ F.1 Baseline Time and Token Cost Analysis ‣ Appendix F Inference Efficiency and Practicality Analysis ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL")
represents a performance-oriented configuration. MARS-SQL allows for
flexible deployment by adjusting the number of generation trajectories
($`N_{g}`$) and validation samples ($`N_{v}`$).
Table [16](#A6.T16 "Table 16 ‣ F.5 Adjustable Cost–Accuracy Trade-offs ‣ Appendix F Inference Efficiency and Practicality Analysis ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL")
illustrates these trade-offs.

| Mode | Params ($`N_{g},N_{v}`$) | Latency | Acc. (%) | Characteristic |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| Fast | (1, 1) | 3.1s | 68.71% | High speed, outperforms SFT |
| Balanced | (4, 4) | 11.5s | 74.90% | Balanced cost-benefit |
| SOTA (Ours) | (8, 8) | 22.1s | 77.84% | Maximum accuracy |
| Over-Sampling | (16, 8) | 42.8s | 77.84% | Diminishing returns |

Table 16: Tunable Cost-Accuracy Curve for MARS-SQL.

Users can select a “Fast” setting to achieve a $`\approx`$3-second
response that still surpasses the greedy SFT baseline, or invest more
computational resources for maximum performance.

We do not claim that MARS-SQL is universally cheaper than every single
larger model. Rather, our claim is that its accuracy gains are not
explained by parameter scaling alone, and that its deployment trade-offs
can be made explicit through latency, token, and VRAM reporting.

### F.6 System-Level Optimization

The latency metrics presented above assume a sequential, single-query
execution, serving as a conservative upper bound. In practical
multi-user deployments, MARS-SQL can achieve higher throughput through
system-level optimizations:

1.  1.
    Pipeline Parallelism: The Grounder, Generator, and Validator agents
    can process different queries in parallel, creating a pipeline for
    incoming requests.
2.  2.
    Batched Validation: The $`N_{g}\times N_{v}`$ validation calls are
    embarrassingly parallel and can be fused into batched requests to
    reduce amortized costs.

[TABLE]

Table 17: Sequential vs. System-Optimized Deployment (Conceptual
Comparison).

Table [17](#A6.T17 "Table 17 ‣ F.6 System-Level Optimization ‣ Appendix F Inference Efficiency and Practicality Analysis ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL")
estimates that with these optimizations, the effective per-query latency
can be reduced by approximately 40–60%, significantly improving
throughput on a single GPU node.

## Appendix G Architecture versus Parameter Scaling

A critical consideration when evaluating multi-agent frameworks is
whether the observed performance improvements are intrinsically tied to
the novel architectural design, or merely a byproduct of increased
parameter capacity at inference time. To decouple our methodological
contributions from pure scaling effects, we conduct three complementary
analyses. First, we benchmark MARS-SQL against a parameter-matched
($`\sim`$21B) ensemble constructed from highly competitive 7B
Text-to-SQL models
(Table [18](#A7.T18 "Table 18 ‣ Appendix G Architecture versus Parameter Scaling ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL")).
Second, we investigate the scaling behavior of the core framework by
expanding the Generation Agent from 7B to 14B parameters, maintaining
the identical Reinforcement Learning (RL) training recipe
(Table [19](#A7.T19 "Table 19 ‣ Appendix G Architecture versus Parameter Scaling ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL")).
Third, to directly address the possibility that a single larger model
could absorb all three roles through increased capacity, we train
single-model multi-task baselines that use one shared model to perform
grounding, generation, and validation
(Table [20](#A7.T20 "Table 20 ‣ Appendix G Architecture versus Parameter Scaling ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL")).

| System Configuration        | Total Parameters | EX Acc. (%) |
|-----------------------------|------------------|-------------|
| Arctic-text2sql-7B (Single) | 7B               | 67.73       |
| SQL-R1 (Single)             | 7B               | 66.03       |
| OmniSQL-7B (Single)         | 7B               | 65.31       |
| SOTA 7B Ensemble (Voting)   | $`\sim`$21B      | 72.10       |
| MARS-SQL (Ours)             | $`\sim`$21B      | 77.84       |

Table 18: Comparison against a strong $`\sim`$21B ensemble on BIRD-dev.
The ensemble combines Arctic-text2sql-7B, SQL-R1, and OmniSQL-7B,
generates eight queries per model, and selects the final answer by
majority voting.

| System Configuration    | Core Model            | EX Acc. (%) | Gain over 7B Base |
|-------------------------|-----------------------|-------------|-------------------|
| Generator Only (Base)   | 7B                    | 66.37       | –                 |
| Generator Only (Scaled) | 14B                   | 67.92       | +1.55             |
| MARS-SQL (Ours)         | 3 $`\times`$ 7B       | 77.84       | +11.47            |
| MARS-SQL (Scaled Gen)   | 14B + 2 $`\times`$ 7B | 78.62       | +12.25            |

Table 19: Scaling the generator versus using multi-agent specialization
on BIRD-dev.

| System Configuration          | Model Size      | EX Acc. (%) |
|-------------------------------|-----------------|-------------|
| Single-model multi-task (SFT) | 14B             | 55.67       |
| Single-model multi-task (SFT) | 32B             | 57.82       |
| MARS-SQL (Ours)               | 3 $`\times`$ 7B | 77.84       |

Table 20: Single-model multi-task baselines on BIRD-dev. A single shared
model is SFT-trained to perform all three roles: grounding, generation,
and validation.

These results support three conclusions. First, as shown in
Table [18](#A7.T18 "Table 18 ‣ Appendix G Architecture versus Parameter Scaling ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL"),
simply stacking three strong 7B Text-to-SQL models into a $`\sim`$21B
ensemble reaches 72.10%, which is still 5.74 points below MARS-SQL.
Second,
Table [19](#A7.T19 "Table 19 ‣ Appendix G Architecture versus Parameter Scaling ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL")
shows that scaling the generator from 7B to 14B improves the
single-agent baseline by only 1.55 points, whereas introducing the
specialized multi-agent workflow improves it by 11.47 points. Third,
Table [20](#A7.T20 "Table 20 ‣ Appendix G Architecture versus Parameter Scaling ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL")
demonstrates that a single shared model trained to absorb all three
roles performs substantially worse even at larger scales: the 14B and
32B multi-task baselines reach only 55.67% and 57.82% EX, respectively.
Together, these findings indicate that the dominant source of
improvement is the role-specialized interactive workflow, not raw
parameter count alone.

## Appendix H Multi-turn Generation

Evolution of Interaction Turns: To understand the impact of RL training
on the agent’s reasoning efficiency, we analyzed the evolution of
rollout lengths during the training process. In our setting, each
“Think–Act–Observe” cycle corresponds to one database interaction turn,
making the average number of interaction turns a proxy for rollout
length.

Grounding Agent (Single-turn): The rollout length (token count)
exhibited a mild U-shaped pattern. Initially, the output became more
concise, followed by a slight lengthening to include only essential
schema information. This reflects a refinement of the policy towards
precise schema selection rather than reasoning from scratch.

Generation Agent (Multi-turn): A distinct trend was observed where the
average number of interaction turns consistently decreased and
stabilized at a lower level. This indicates that the agent learned to
solve problems more directly and recognized when to terminate the search
efficiently. This efficiency gain is quantitatively supported by the
evaluation on the BIRD-dev set (with a maximum of 5 turns), as shown in
Table [21](#A8.T21 "Table 21 ‣ Appendix H Multi-turn Generation ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL").
The RL-trained agent significantly reduces the average turns across all
difficulty levels compared to the base model.

| Model | Avg. Turns (Challenging) | Avg. Turns (Moderate) | Avg. Turns (Simple) |
|----|----|----|----|
| Before RL (Base Model) | 2.90 | 2.67 | 2.27 |
| After RL (Generation Agent) | 1.82 | 1.71 | 1.45 |

Table 21: Comparison of Average Interaction Turns on BIRD-dev (Max Turns
= 5) before and after RL training.

|                         |                |
|-------------------------|----------------|
| \# of Interaction Turns | \# of Examples |
| 1                       | 1,116          |
| 2                       | 174            |
| 3                       | 105            |
| 4                       | 88             |
| 5+                      | 51             |

Table 22: Distribution of Interaction Turns Used by the Generation Agent
on BIRD-dev.

Furthermore, analyzing the specific distribution of turns reveals that
the agent learns an adaptive and non-wasteful strategy. As presented in
Table [22](#A8.T22 "Table 22 ‣ Appendix H Multi-turn Generation ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL"),
while the agent retains the capacity to use multiple turns for complex
reasoning, it solves the vast majority of problems (1,116 cases) in a
single interaction. Crucially, for the ”long-tail” of more difficult
queries, the agent robustly applies deeper reasoning, utilizing up to 5
or more turns to arrive at the correct solution. This distribution
confirms that the agent is not bound by arbitrary limits but instead
dynamically decides the necessary reasoning depth for each specific
query.

Figure [6](#A8.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Appendix H Multi-turn Generation ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL")
provides a concrete example of the agent’s interactive and
self-correcting workflow. The agent initially generates a query with a
typographical error in a table name ‘fprm’. Upon receiving an
‘OperationalError’ from the database, it correctly identifies the
mistake in its next thought process, corrects the table name to ‘frpm’,
and re-executes the query. The second attempt returns an empty result,
prompting the agent to re-evaluate its filtering logic. It deduces that
it incorrectly used a district name as a county name and refines the
‘WHERE’ clause accordingly. This final attempt successfully retrieves
the correct data, leading the agent to output the validated query as its
final solution.

![Refer to caption](2511.01008v2/Interactive_Process.png)

Figure 6: Example of interactive process in the generation.

## Appendix I Qualitative Analysis: Reasoning Beyond Valid Execution

A core feature of our Generation Agent is its learned policy to evaluate
the semantic content and plausibility of execution results, rather than
merely checking for syntax errors. This allows the agent to continue
reasoning even when the database returns a non-empty, non-error result.
Below, we present two real-world case studies from the BIRD-dev set
illustrating this capability.

### I.1 Scenario 1: Complex Problem Decomposition

In complex queries, a successful execution often represents only an
intermediate step in a larger plan. The agent effectively decomposes the
problem, using the observation from the first step to inform the
subsequent logic.

Question: Consider the average difference between K-12 enrollment and
15-17 enrollment of schools that are locally funded, list the names and
DOC type of schools which has a difference above this average.

Turn 1 (Think): To solve this problem, I need to follow these steps: 1)
Calculate the average difference between K-12 enrollment and 15-17
enrollment for all schools. 2) Filter the schools based on the funding
type. 3) Calculate the difference for filtered schools. 4) Identify
schools above the average.

Turn 1 (SQL):

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,U0VMRUNUIEFWRygiRW5yb2xsbWVudCAoSy0xMikiIC0gIkVucm9sbG1lbnQgKEFnZXMgNS0xNykiKSBGUk9NIGZycG07)

SELECT AVG("Enrollment (K-12)" - "Enrollment (Ages 5-17)") FROM frpm;

Turn 1 (Observation): 16.261833

Turn 2 (Think): (The agent recognizes this is an intermediate value, not
the final answer.) The average difference is approximately 16.26. Now, I
will filter the schools based on the funding type (locally funded) and
calculate the difference for these schools against this average.

Turn 2 (SQL):

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,U0VMRUNUIFQyLlNjaG9vbCwgVDIuRE9DIEZST00gZnJwbSBBUyBUMSBKT0lOIHNjaG9vbHMgQVMgVDIgT04gVDEuQ0RTQ29kZSA9IFQyLkNEU0NvZGUgV0hFUkUgVDIuRnVuZGluZ1R5cGUgPSAnTG9jYWxseSBmdW5kZWQnIEFORCAoVDEuIkVucm9sbG1lbnQgKEstMTIpIiAtIFQxLiJFbnJvbGxtZW50IChBZ2VzIDUtMTcpIikgPiAxNi4yNjs=)

SELECT T2.School, T2.DOC FROM frpm AS T1 JOIN schools AS T2 ON
T1.CDSCode = T2.CDSCode WHERE T2.FundingType = ’Locally funded’ AND
(T1."Enrollment (K-12)" - T1."Enrollment (Ages 5-17)") \> 16.26;

Turn 2 (Observation): \[(‘Circle of Independent Learning’, ‘54’),
(‘Learning Community Charter’, ‘00’)\]

Turn 3 (Think): The query executed successfully and returned non-empty
results. I will now combine the logic into a single nested query for the
final answer.

Turn 3 (Final Solution):

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

SELECT T2.School, T2.DOC FROM frpm AS T1 INNER JOIN schools AS T2 ON
T1.CDSCode = T2.CDSCode WHERE T2.FundingType = ’Locally funded’ AND
(T1."Enrollment (K-12)" - T1."Enrollment (Ages 5-17)") \> (SELECT
AVG(T3."Enrollment (K-12)" - T3."Enrollment (Ages 5-17)") FROM frpm AS
T3 INNER JOIN schools AS T4 ON T3.CDSCode = T4.CDSCode WHERE
T4.FundingType = ’Locally funded’)

### I.2 Scenario 2: Data Plausibility and Sanity Checking

The agent also learns to perform “sanity checks.” If a syntactically
correct query returns implausible data (e.g., placeholder values), the
agent triggers a self-correction loop to verify and refine the query
before finalizing the answer.

Question: Which cities have the top 5 lowest enrollment number for
students in grades 1 through 12?

Turn 1 (Think): I need to find the cities with the top 5 lowest
enrollment numbers. I will join the tables and order by enrollment
ascending.

Turn 1 (SQL):

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,U0VMRUNUIFQyLkNpdHksIFQxLiJFbnJvbGxtZW50IChLLTEyKSIgRlJPTSBmcnBtIEFTIFQxIElOTkVSIEpPSU4gc2Nob29scyBBUyBUMiBPTiBUMS5DRFNDb2RlID0gVDIuQ0RTQ29kZSBPUkRFUiBCWSBUMS4iRW5yb2xsbWVudCAoSy0xMikiIEFTQyBMSU1JVCA1Ow==)

SELECT T2.City, T1."Enrollment (K-12)" FROM frpm AS T1 INNER JOIN
schools AS T2 ON T1.CDSCode = T2.CDSCode ORDER BY T1."Enrollment (K-12)"
ASC LIMIT 5;

Turn 1 (Observation): \[(‘Markleeville’, 1.0), (‘Oakland’, 1.0),
(‘Palermo’, 1.0)\]

Turn 2 (Think): (The agent detects a potential data anomaly.) The result
shows enrollment numbers are very low (1.0), which might indicate an
error in the data or the need to filter out non-enrollment entries.
Let’s check the data to ensure accuracy.

Turn 2 (SQL):

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,U0VMRUNUIENEU0NvZGUgRlJPTSBmcnBtIFdIRVJFICJFbnJvbGxtZW50IChLLTEyKSIgIT0gMS4wIExJTUlUIDEwOw==)

SELECT CDSCode FROM frpm WHERE "Enrollment (K-12)" != 1.0 LIMIT 10;

Turn 2 (Observation): \[(‘01100170130419’), (‘01100170112607’)...\]

Turn 3 (Think): The check confirms that there are legitimate records
with other values, and ’1.0’ likely represents missing or placeholder
data. I need to filter these out to get accurate city names.

Turn 3 (SQL):

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,U0VMRUNUIFQyLkNpdHkgRlJPTSBmcnBtIEFTIFQxIElOTkVSIEpPSU4gc2Nob29scyBBUyBUMiBPTiBUMS5DRFNDb2RlID0gVDIuQ0RTQ29kZSBXSEVSRSBUMS4iRW5yb2xsbWVudCAoSy0xMikiICE9IDEuMCBPUkRFUiBCWSBUMS4iRW5yb2xsbWVudCAoSy0xMikiIEFTQyBMSU1JVCA1Ow==)

SELECT T2.City FROM frpm AS T1 INNER JOIN schools AS T2 ON T1.CDSCode =
T2.CDSCode WHERE T1."Enrollment (K-12)" != 1.0 ORDER BY T1."Enrollment
(K-12)" ASC LIMIT 5;

Turn 3 (Observation): \[(‘Bishop’), (‘Kingsburg’), (‘Oakland’),
(‘Williams’), (‘Compton’)\]

Turn 4 (Think): Now, the cities with the lowest enrollment numbers are
identified and the data looks plausible. I can provide the final SQL
query.

Turn 4 (Final Solution):

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,U0VMRUNUIFQyLkNpdHkgRlJPTSBmcnBtIEFTIFQxIElOTkVSIEpPSU4gc2Nob29scyBBUyBUMiBPTiBUMS5DRFNDb2RlID0gVDIuQ0RTQ29kZSBXSEVSRSBUMS4iRW5yb2xsbWVudCAoSy0xMikiICE9IDEuMCBPUkRFUiBCWSBUMS4iRW5yb2xsbWVudCAoSy0xMikiIEFTQyBMSU1JVCA1Ow==)

SELECT T2.City FROM frpm AS T1 INNER JOIN schools AS T2 ON T1.CDSCode =
T2.CDSCode WHERE T1."Enrollment (K-12)" != 1.0 ORDER BY T1."Enrollment
(K-12)" ASC LIMIT 5;

### I.3 Scenario 3: Overcoming Sub-optimal Logic and Boundary Errors

This case demonstrates the agent’s ability to recover from hidden
logical and semantic errors, specifically regarding boundary conditions
and offset calculations. Even when a query executes perfectly without
syntax errors, the agent evaluates the mathematical alignment between
its SQL logic and the user’s intent, iteratively refining its approach
to overcome sub-optimal reasoning.

Question: What is the eligible free rate of the 10th and 11th schools
with the highest enrolment for students in grades 1 through 12?

Turn 1 (Think): The question asks for the eligible free rate for the
10th and 11th schools based on enrollment. I need to calculate this
rate, sort the schools by enrollment in descending order, and select the
10th and 11th positions. I will use the LIMIT clause to extract these
two specific rows.

Turn 1 (SQL):

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,U0VMRUNUICJGcmVlIE1lYWwgQ291bnQgKEstMTIpIiAvICJFbnJvbGxtZW50IChLLTEyKSIgYXMgcmF0ZSBGUk9NIGZycG0gT1JERVIgQlkgIkVucm9sbG1lbnQgKEstMTIpIiBERVNDIExJTUlUIDEsIDI7)

SELECT "Free Meal Count (K-12)" / "Enrollment (K-12)" as rate FROM frpm
ORDER BY "Enrollment (K-12)" DESC LIMIT 1, 2;

Turn 1 (Observation): \[(0.815746,), (0.338349,)\]

Turn 2 (Think): (The agent detects a sub-optimal logic in pagination.)
The query successfully returned results, but the logic LIMIT 1, 2 is
incorrect for finding the 10th and 11th schools. In SQL, the offset
starts at 0, so an offset of 1 skips only the 1st row and returns the
2nd and 3rd rows. Furthermore, to prevent potential integer division
truncation, I should cast the numerator to a real number. I need to
adjust the offset to 9 to correctly target the 10th and 11th schools.

Turn 2 (SQL):

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,U0VMRUNUIENBU1QoIkZyZWUgTWVhbCBDb3VudCAoSy0xMikiIEFTIFJFQUwpIC8gIkVucm9sbG1lbnQgKEstMTIpIiBhcyByYXRlIEZST00gZnJwbSBPUkRFUiBCWSAiRW5yb2xsbWVudCAoSy0xMikiIERFU0MgTElNSVQgOSwgMjs=)

SELECT CAST("Free Meal Count (K-12)" AS REAL) / "Enrollment (K-12)" as
rate FROM frpm ORDER BY "Enrollment (K-12)" DESC LIMIT 9, 2;

Turn 2 (Observation): \[(0.134436,), (0.290589,)\]

Turn 3 (Think): The query now orders the rates by enrollment in
descending order and uses the correct pagination boundary. LIMIT 9, 2
correctly skips the top 9 schools and selects the 10th and 11th rows.
The data type casting also ensures robust calculation. The results are
now logical and correct.

Turn 3 (Final Solution):

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,U0VMRUNUIENBU1QoIkZyZWUgTWVhbCBDb3VudCAoSy0xMikiIEFTIFJFQUwpIC8gIkVucm9sbG1lbnQgKEstMTIpIiBGUk9NIGZycG0gT1JERVIgQlkgIkVucm9sbG1lbnQgKEstMTIpIiBERVNDIExJTUlUIDksIDI7)

SELECT CAST("Free Meal Count (K-12)" AS REAL) / "Enrollment (K-12)" FROM
frpm ORDER BY "Enrollment (K-12)" DESC LIMIT 9, 2;

### I.4 Scenario 4: Recovery from Schema Hallucination and Ambiguity

This case illustrates the agent’s capacity to recover from schema
hallucinations (e.g., mistyping or misremembering table names) and
simultaneously resolve semantic ambiguities. When confronted with a
database execution error, the agent not only corrects the structural
typo but also proactively refines the logical filtering conditions based
on a deeper understanding of the schema constraints.

Question: Please list the zip code of all the charter schools in Fresno
County Office of Education.

Turn 1 (Think): I need to retrieve the zip codes of all charter schools
within the Fresno County Office of Education. I will join the schools
table with the fprm table on the CDSCode and filter by the county and
charter school status.

Turn 1 (SQL):

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,U0VMRUNUIFQxLlppcCBGUk9NIHNjaG9vbHMgQVMgVDEgSU5ORVIgSk9JTiBmcHJtIEFTIFQyIE9OIFQxLkNEU0NvZGUgPSBUMi5DRFNDb2RlIFdIRVJFIFQxLkNvdW50eSA9ICdGcmVzbm8gQ291bnR5IE9mZmljZSBvZiBFZHVjYXRpb24nIEFORCBUMi4iQ2hhcnRlciBTY2hvb2wgKFkvTikiID0gMTs=)

SELECT T1.Zip FROM schools AS T1 INNER JOIN fprm AS T2 ON T1.CDSCode =
T2.CDSCode WHERE T1.County = ’Fresno County Office of Education’ AND
T2."Charter School (Y/N)" = 1;

Turn 1 (Observation): Operational Error: no such table: fprm

Turn 2 (Think): (The agent processes the database error and reviews the
schema.) I made a typo in the table name; it should be frpm instead of
fprm. Furthermore, ’Fresno County Office of Education’ likely refers to
the school District rather than the County itself, as the county name is
typically just ’Fresno’. I will correct the table hallucination and
refine the WHERE clause to check both County and District for precise
filtering.

Turn 2 (SQL):

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,U0VMRUNUIFQxLlppcCBGUk9NIHNjaG9vbHMgQVMgVDEgSU5ORVIgSk9JTiBmcnBtIEFTIFQyIE9OIFQxLkNEU0NvZGUgPSBUMi5DRFNDb2RlIFdIRVJFIFQyLiJDaGFydGVyIFNjaG9vbCAoWS9OKSIgPSAxIEFORCBUMS5Db3VudHkgPSAnRnJlc25vJyBBTkQgVDEuRGlzdHJpY3QgPSAnRnJlc25vIENvdW50eSBPZmZpY2Ugb2YgRWR1Y2F0aW9uJzs=)

SELECT T1.Zip FROM schools AS T1 INNER JOIN frpm AS T2 ON T1.CDSCode =
T2.CDSCode WHERE T2."Charter School (Y/N)" = 1 AND T1.County = ’Fresno’
AND T1.District = ’Fresno County Office of Education’;

Turn 2 (Observation): \[(’93726-5309’,), (’93628-9602’,),
(’93706-2611’,), (’93726-5208’,), (’93706-2819’,)\]

Turn 3 (Think): The query executed successfully and returned a valid
list of zip codes. The table name was correctly resolved, and the
district/county filtering accurately identified the target schools. I
can now provide the final solution.

Turn 3 (Final Solution):

## Appendix J Dataset-Wide Controlled Isolation

To complement the component ablation in the main paper, we perform a
dataset-wide controlled-isolation analysis on the full BIRD-dev set
(1,534 queries). The goal is to quantify how many additional queries are
resolved by each mechanism when starting from a strict baseline. We use
the RL Generator only with $`T{=}1`$ and greedy decoding as the baseline
configuration, which achieves 62.78% execution accuracy.

| Configuration / Mechanism | Extra Solved Cases | Gain |
|----|----|----|
| Strict baseline: RL Generator only ($`T{=}1`$, Greedy) | — | 62.78% EX |
| + Schema pruning | 56 | +3.63% |
| + RL interactive reasoning | 44 | +2.89% |
| + Generative verification / reranking | 131 | +8.54% |
| Full MARS-SQL | 231 | 77.84% EX |

Table 23: Dataset-wide controlled isolation on BIRD-dev. Each row
attributes additional solved queries beyond the strict RL-Generator
baseline.

Two observations follow from
Table [23](#A10.T23 "Table 23 ‣ Appendix J Dataset-Wide Controlled Isolation ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL").
First, generative verification is the single largest isolated
contributor, which is consistent with the strong gains observed in our
selection-method analysis. Second, the RL interactive policy contributes
44 additional correct queries under greedy decoding alone, without any
sampling or reranking. This directly supports our claim that the model
has learned to use execution feedback for self-correction at the policy
level, rather than benefiting only from test-time selection.

interaction turns (T) allowed during training and inference. The study
compares the performance of the base model against versions fine-tuned
with maximum turn limits of T=1, T=5, and T=10. For each training
configuration, we report three execution accuracy metrics on the
BIRD-dev benchmark: Greedy (a single output), Best of 8 (the highest
score among 8 candidates), and Selected (the score after reranking). The
results indicate that increasing the number of turns during fine-tuning
consistently improves performance. For example, the model trained with
T=10 achieves the highest Greedy (69.88%) and Best of 8 (83.89%)
accuracy when inferring with 10 turns, demonstrating the value of a
larger interaction budget for complex reasoning.

## Appendix M Table Level Grounding

Table [26](#A13.T26 "Table 26 ‣ Appendix M Table Level Grounding ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL")
details the prompt for our RL-trained Schema Grounding Agent, which
elicit a step-by-step reasoning process during inference. It instructs
the agent to analyze a given table’s schema in the context of the user’s
question and any external knowledge. The agent is required to first
articulate its analysis within ‘$`<`$think$`>`$’ tags, followed by a
final, parsable decision in ‘$`<`$answer$`>`$’ tags. This output must
specify the table’s relevance (‘Y’/‘N’) and, if applicable, a Python
list of useful columns. This structured format ensures a transparent and
predictable output format crucial for our framework.

Table 26: The prompt used to guide the agent in the table-level schema
linking task. It includes the role description, task instructions,
output format examples, and the prefix for the agent’s response.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Table [27](#A13.T27 "Table 27 ‣ Appendix M Table Level Grounding ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL")
presents recall and precision statistics for our schema grounding agent,
comparing our RL-based approach against the base model and a version
trained with Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT). The results clearly
demonstrate the superiority of our method, which achieves exceptionally
high recall and precision across all benchmarks. On the complex
in-domain BIRD-dev set, our primary concern is recall. Our agent
achieves a recall of 97.78%, with only 48 examples failing to identify
all required schema components, which we consider a highly effective
result. Simultaneously, it maintains a high precision of 90.74%,
indicating that the selections are not only comprehensive but also
accurate. This strong performance extends to the out-of-domain
Spider-test and Spider-DK benchmarks, underscoring the robustness of our
RL-trained grounding agent.

| Grounding Model | Bird dev |  | Spider test |  | Spider DK |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | Recall (%) | Precision (%) | Recall (%) | Precision (%) | Recall (%) | Precision (%) |
| Qwen 7B (Base) | 68.59 | 53.45 | 87.48 | 69.22 | 84.25 | 66.54 |
| Qwen 7B + SFT | 74.97 | 67.01 | 90.39 | 78.16 | 88.60 | 72.71 |
| Qwen 7B + RL (Ours) | 97.78 | 90.74 | 98.97 | 93.62 | 98.13 | 91.59 |

Table 27: Recall and precision statistics after grounding for Bird-dev,
Spider-test and Spider-DK. Recall measures the percentage of instances
where all required columns were identified. Precision measures the ratio
of required columns to all selected columns, indicating the selection’s
accuracy.

The practical impact of the Grounding Agent depends on the schema
regime. On smaller and cleaner schemas such as Spider, the Generator can
often operate with comparatively limited interference, so the end-to-end
gain from grounding is smaller. On BIRD-dev, however, the search space
is much larger, making schema filtering substantially more valuable.
More broadly, this requirement to preserve salient evidence while
filtering large amounts of irrelevant context is also consistent with
observations from long-form and long-context analysis ([He et al.,
2026](#bib.bib3)).
Table [28](#A13.T28 "Table 28 ‣ Appendix M Table Level Grounding ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL")
summarizes this contrast.

| Dataset  | Avg. Schema Tokens | Avg. Columns/DB | Avg. Tokens/SQL |
|----------|--------------------|-----------------|-----------------|
| Spider   | $`\sim`$250        | 26.82           | 30.9            |
| BIRD-dev | $`\sim`$950        | 54.56           | 18.5            |

Table 28: Dataset characteristics relevant to the Grounding Agent.
Larger schemas create more distractors for downstream generation.

This context also helps explain why the Grounder is more important under
semantic ambiguity and domain shift. Spider-DK is specifically designed
to break clean lexical matches between questions and schemas, and
Table [27](#A13.T27 "Table 27 ‣ Appendix M Table Level Grounding ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL")
shows that our RL Grounder maintains very high recall and precision
there as well. In this sense, grounding is best understood not as a
uniformly large gain on every benchmark, but as a component whose
importance increases with schema scale, ambiguity, and cross-domain
difficulty.

## Appendix N Generation Agent Prompt

Table [29](#A14.T29 "Table 29 ‣ Appendix N Generation Agent Prompt ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL")
details the comprehensive prompt structure used to guide the agent’s
multi-turn generation process. The prompt establishes the agent’s
persona as a data science expert and provides all necessary context,
including the database schema, external knowledge, and the user’s
question. It strictly enforces an output format that requires the agent
to vocalize its reasoning within $`<`$think$`>`$ blocks before executing
a query in a $`<`$sql$`>`$ block. The database returns feedback in an
$`<`$observation$`>`$ block, which the agent uses for subsequent
reasoning turns, ultimately providing the final answer in a
$`<`$solution$`>`$ block. This iterative structure is designed to
facilitate a dynamic, step-by-step problem-solving process.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Table 29: Prompt example for SQL reasoning without memory.

## Appendix O Validation Agent

Our Generative Validation Agent is guided by the prompt detailed in
Table [30](#A15.T30 "Table 30 ‣ Appendix O Validation Agent ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL").
The prompt instructs the agent to act as an expert SQL data analyst,
with the objective of evaluating the logical correctness of a proposed
SQL solution for a given problem. Unlike our previous approach, this
prompt no longer constrains the agent to reason about a sampled or
truncated database. Instead, it assumes the agent evaluates the query’s
validity against the full database schema and context. The prompt
structure provides the agent with the user’s question, the candidate SQL
solution, and a dedicated field for any relevant “External Knowledge”
that might be necessary for a correct evaluation. The output format
remains strict, requiring the agent to begin its response with a
definitive “Yes” or “No” before any subsequent reasoning.

Table 30: The prompt used for the Generative Validation Agent. The agent
is framed as a SQL expert and is provided with the problem, the proposed
SQL query, and any relevant external knowledge. It evaluates the logical
correctness of the query and must provide a final “Yes” or “No”
judgment.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Appendix P LLM as a judge prompt

The prompt in
Table [31](#A16.T31 "Table 31 ‣ Appendix P LLM as a judge prompt ‣ MARS-SQL: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning FrameworkFor Text-To-SQL")
is used for our baseline selection method LLM as a judge. This prompt is
designed to guide the model in identifying the optimal SQL query from a
set of generated candidates. The agent is explicitly instructed to
consider each candidate’s associated reasoning, the SQL query itself,
and most crucially, its execution observation on the database. This
emphasis on execution results is paramount, as it allows the agent to
distinguish between syntactically correct queries and those that truly
provide the correct and complete answer to the user’s question, even if
a query might appear correct but yields erroneous or empty results.
After presenting the user’s question and the formatted candidate
solutions (each including reasoning, SQL, and execution output), the
prompt concludes with strict instructions for the agent to output only
the index number of the single best candidate. In cases of ties, the
candidate with the lowest index is to be chosen, ensuring a
deterministic selection process.

Table 31: The prompt used for the Selection Agent, operating as an LLM
judge. It guides the model to select the best SQL query from multiple
candidates by evaluating their reasoning, SQL code, and critically,
their execution observations. Strict output instructions ensure a direct
index selection.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
